A piano note is a point: one fixed pitch. A blue note is more like an **area**, a range of
pitch the player moves around in. Kubik calls these "flexible pitch areas" and Titon "pitch
complexes". Charalampidis says some blues players call the moving around "pitch shading" or
"worrying the notes".

**How to use the page.** Start the **Drone** or **Power chord vamp** (bar at the bottom).
Press and drag along each strip to play any pitch in the range. The readout gives the distance
from the nearest piano key in **cents** (100 cents = one semitone). The buttons play the ways
of reaching each area.

## What early listeners wrote

Hein quotes two early collections of African American music:

- *Slave Songs of the United States* (1867) says the singers made sounds that "cannot be
  precisely represented by the gamut", and it describes their slides.
- Thomas Fenner, *Hampton and Its Students* (1874), describes tones that musical notation has no
  signs for, sung "as nearly as possible by the flat seventh", and rarely discordant.

## The 3rd

Peter van der Merwe says most blues 3rds are **neutral** in practice, between minor and major.
He lists the degrees that get flattened by a quarter tone or a semitone, most often first:
the **3rd, 7th, 5th, 6th**.

<div class="bz" data-w="zone" data-deg="3" data-title="The 3rd's area"></div>

Charalampidis's main point is that a blues player hears this whole area as **one note** (one
*toneme*). The ♭3 and the 3 are not two different notes. They are two shades of the same 3rd.

## The 4th, ♯4 and 5th

Court Cutting analysed 15 early blues recordings by computer. He found three clusters of blue
pitch: the neutral 3rd, a cluster **between 4 and ♯4**, and one **around ♭7**. Charalampidis
plays the 4th a little sharp, bends up to just below ♯4, and plays the 5th a little flat,
almost always reached by a bend from the 4th.

<div class="bz" data-w="zone" data-deg="45" data-title="The 4th to the 5th"></div>

## The 7th

Charalampidis describes two 7ths. One is a little **above** the piano's ♭7, sometimes as high as
the neutral 7th. The other is a little **below** it, reached by bending up from the 5th or the
6th, and usually followed by the 6th.

<div class="bz" data-w="zone" data-deg="7" data-title="The 7th's area"></div>

## Important notes and passing notes

Not every note is shaded. Van der Merwe calls the blues mode a "modal frame": a framework of
melodically sensitive notes with less important notes between them. On a fixed-pitch
instrument, the passing notes are often plain piano pitches. Hein puts it another way: the
scale is a set of **islands** in a continuous sea of pitch.

To play quarter tones on a grid, try the pitch pads in [Tuning Systems](tuning-systems.qmd)
(section *24 notes*). Bending technique on the guitar is in [Guitar Bends](guitar-bends.qmd).
